title: Jesus - our High Priest
summary: The earthly sanctuary was a model of the plan of salvation: its sacrifices pointed to Jesus the Lamb, and its priesthood to his ministry. Today Jesus is the High Priest in the heavenly sanctuary - our only Mediator. The sanctuary is linked with the covenant: the law in the ark, grace on the mercy seat; we have sure access to God.

sections.heading: The Sanctuary as God's Model of Salvation

items.comment: God asks for a sanctuary, "that he may dwell among" the people, and commands it to be built "according to the pattern." This is not a human idea of religion - it is God's plan, picturing how God wants to be with humanity.

questions.text: What does God mainly desire in asking for a sanctuary - ritual, or dwelling among his people?

items.comment: The earthly sanctuary was "a copy and shadow" of the heavenly reality. It is a model that teaches - it points to something greater than itself.

questions.text: If the sanctuary is a "shadow," then what reality is it meant to point to?

items.comment: "Your way, O God, is in the sanctuary" - the sanctuary presents the way in which God saves humanity. Every part of it means something.

questions.text: What does it mean that God reveals his "way" of salvation through objects and rituals?

items.label: "sanctuary": mishkan and miqdash
items.content: The Bible uses two main words for the sanctuary: *mishkan* ("dwelling," from a root meaning "to dwell, to abide") and *miqdash* ("holy place," from "holy"). Together they convey the heart of it: the holy God desires to dwell among his people. The command in Exod 25:8 says it directly: "Make me a sanctuary, that I may dwell among them." Significantly, the request for a sanctuary comes only after the exodus from Egypt and the making of the covenant - redemption precedes access to the sanctuary.

questions.text: If God "made a sanctuary, that he may dwell among them," what does that say about what he desires most toward you?

items.label: the structure of the sanctuary and the plan of salvation
items.content: The courtyard (the altar of sacrifice, the laver), the holy place (the bread, the lampstand, the altar of incense), and the most holy place (the ark) are sometimes read as successive stages of salvation: the sacrifice/cross, daily intercession and fellowship, and finally judgment and the fullness of God's presence. The sanctuary is thus a clear "diagram" of the gospel.

items.label: "according to the pattern" (tabnit)
items.content: Moses was to build the sanctuary "according to the pattern" shown to him on the mountain (Exod 25:9, 40). The Hebrew *tabnit* (from "to build") means a model or representation of something, which normally presupposes the existence of an original. Note that this original is the heavenly sanctuary: the earthly one is its "copy and shadow" (Heb 8:5), pointing beyond itself.

questions.text: What changes in how we view the earthly rituals when we realize they are a "shadow" of a real, heavenly reality?

items.comment: The sinner laid a hand on the animal, confessed the guilt, and it died in his place. The picture is clear: sin leads to death, but someone innocent can take my place.

questions.text: What was the heart of a person meant to understand as he pointed with his own hand to the sacrifice dying in his stead?

items.comment: John points to Jesus: "the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world." All the slain lambs pointed to this one - the true Sacrifice.

questions.text: If every sacrifice was a foreshadowing, then what happened when Jesus the Lamb came?

items.comment: Centuries earlier the prophet describes the Servant, on whom "the LORD laid the iniquity of us all." This is the heart of the sacrificial system: substitution.

questions.text: Which words in this text speak most powerfully that someone bore the punishment in your place?

items.comment: We were ransomed "with the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb." The language of the sanctuary is transferred directly to Jesus - he is the reality of the sacrifices.

questions.text: What does the price God paid for a person's ransom say about that person's worth?

items.label: "once for all"
items.content: The Letter to the Hebrews emphasizes that the repeated animal sacrifices "could not take away sins" (Heb 10:4); they were only a shadow. Christ, on the other hand, offered himself "once for all" (Heb 7:27; 10:10) and "by his own blood" entered "once for all into the holy place, having obtained eternal redemption" (Heb 9:12). The cross is perfect and unrepeatable - nothing needs to be added to it.

questions.text: Since the sacrifice of Jesus was offered "once for all," what do you no longer have to add in order to be accepted by God?

sections.heading: Jesus, Our High Priest in Heaven

items.comment: We have "a great High Priest who has passed through the heavens" and who sympathizes with our weaknesses. That is why we can "come boldly to the throne of grace." Here the priest is not a guardian of distance, but the one who opens access.

questions.text: What changes in prayer when we realize that the High Priest understands your weakness and does not condemn?

items.comment: Jesus "always lives to intercede" for us, and therefore is able to "save completely." His mediation is unceasing and effective to the end.

questions.text: What gives the assurance that Jesus can save "completely," and not only in part?

items.label: a priest "after the order of Melchizedek"
items.content: Heb 7 demonstrates the superiority of Christ's priesthood, reaching back to Ps 110:4: "You are a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek." Jesus is a priest not by virtue of descent from the line of Aaron (he was not a Levite), but "by the power of an indestructible life" and by God's oath. That is why his priesthood is imperishable - since it "continues forever," he can save completely.

questions.text: What does it mean for your security that Jesus is a High Priest "forever," whose ministry will never end?

items.comment: When we fall, "we have an Advocate with the Father - Jesus Christ the righteous." We have a Defender, not an accuser.

questions.text: According to this text, who is on your side when you sin - and how does that affect feelings of guilt?

items.comment: Jesus "sat down at the right hand" and ministers in "the true tabernacle, set up by the Lord." The heavenly sanctuary is not a metaphor - it is the real place of his ministry for us.

questions.text: What does it mean to you that Jesus now carries out a concrete ministry for you in heaven?
Since Jesus understands us, always lives, and never turns away those who come, what would he lack that would make an additional mediator necessary?

sections.heading: The Sanctuary Joined to the Covenant

items.comment: At the heart of the sanctuary, in the ark, was placed the "Testimony" - the tablets of the Ten Commandments. God's law is at the very center of the sanctuary: it is the foundation of the covenant.

questions.text: What does it mean that God's law is found at the very heart of the sanctuary?

items.comment: Above the law, on the ark, lies the "mercy seat" (the cover of atonement), where God meets with his people. Above the law is grace - justice and mercy meet exactly where God speaks to humanity.

questions.text: What does the picture say about God: the law inside the ark, and above it the place of atonement and meeting?

items.label: "mercy seat" (kappōret / hilastērion)
items.content: The Hebrew *kappōret* (the cover of the ark) is connected with a root meaning "to cover, to make atonement"; the Septuagint and the New Testament use *hilastērion* (Rom 3:25 applies it to Christ). The place where blood covered the law becomes a picture of Christ, in whom justice and mercy meet.

questions.text: How does the picture of "covering the law with blood" help us understand what atonement in Christ is?

items.comment: Jesus, as High Priest, entered with his own blood and became "the mediator of a new covenant." The sanctuary and the covenant are one: the Mediator guarantees that law and grace are not opposed to each other.

questions.text: How does Jesus unite in himself both the law (justice) and grace (forgiveness)?

items.comment: Through the blood of Jesus we have "bold access" to the most holy place and can "draw near with full assurance of faith." The veil that once barred the way has been opened.

questions.text: What changes in your relationship with God in the truth that access to him is now open and sure?

items.label: the torn veil
items.content: At the moment of Jesus' death the veil of the temple "was torn in two, from top to bottom" (Matt 27:51). In the sanctuary the veil separated the holy place from the most holy and guarded the distance. Its tearing - and precisely at the moment of Christ's sacrifice - pictures that through his blood the way to God has been opened; this is the same truth proclaimed in Heb 10:19-20 about "a new and living way through the veil."

questions.text: What does it mean for your prayer that the veil separating you from God was torn "from the top" - by God's initiative?

sections.heading: The Phase of Judgment: Good News (a callback to "The Hour of Judgment")

items.comment: Daniel sees a throne, opened books, and the court seated. In the context of the sanctuary this is not a scene of terror - it is the moment when the case of God's people is settled. (A reference to the study "The Hour of Judgment.")

questions.text: Must judgment arouse fear, if your Judge is at the same time your Defender?

items.comment: The "Son of Man" comes before the Ancient of Days and receives a kingdom. In the scene of judgment the central figure is Jesus - the One who represents us.

questions.text: Who stands at the center of the judgment scene, and what does that mean for someone who has trusted him?

items.comment: Christ entered "into the presence of God on our behalf." In the phase of judgment Jesus is not an accuser - he stands there as our representative.

questions.text: What does it mean that Jesus stands before God "on our behalf," precisely at the time of judgment?

items.label: the Day of Atonement (Lev 16)
items.content: Once a year the high priest entered the most holy place to perform the final cleansing of the sanctuary "from the uncleannesses and transgressions" of the people (Lev 16). It was a day of cleansing and at the same time of judgment: God assessed who truly relies on his grace. The two phases of the earthly ministry - the daily one and the one on the Day of Atonement - correspond to two aspects of Christ's ministry: unceasing intercession and the work of judgment/cleansing (cf. Heb 9:23). For those who trust in Jesus this is not a threat, but the final confirmation that their sins have been removed.

questions.text: Since the Day of Atonement settled the matter of sin in favor of God's people, why can the phase of judgment be good news for you?

application.text: The sanctuary is God's picture of the whole way of salvation. The sacrifices pointed to Jesus the Lamb, who died in my place. Today this same Jesus is my High Priest in heaven - he unceasingly intercedes for me and gives me sure, open access to God. At the heart of the sanctuary the law (justice) meets grace (forgiveness), and one Mediator unites them. Even judgment need not terrify: my Judge is my Defender. I need no one else between myself and God - I have Jesus, and that is enough.
application.challenge: This week, with every prayer, deliberately turn to God "through Jesus, my High Priest." Once, confess to him a specific sin outright and accept that you have an Advocate, not an accuser (1 John 2:1) - and write down how it changes your sense of access to God.
